title: Peter Damian (21 February)
hookLine: a monk and reformer who wrote blunt letters against corruption in the Church

lines: THREE Versions OF A HARD LETTER.
A MONK PULLED FROM HIS CELL.
cards: Some letters you write three times. The first version is furious. The second is so polite it says nothing.
The third, if you're lucky, says the true thing plainly, because you care about the person reading it. Peter Damian spent much of his life writing the third kind.

A monk in Italy who loved silence and his hermit's cell, he kept being pulled out of it to tell bishops, priests and even popes what they did not want to hear. He signed himself, tradition says, Peter the sinner, monk.

teach.h: A SWINEHERD BOY, THEN A HERMIT.
teach.b: Tradition says Peter Damian began poor. An orphan, he was taken in by relatives and set to work as a boy looking after pigs, until an older brother saw how bright he was and paid for his schooling.

He became a teacher, then left it all for a hermitage, where the monks lived in small cells and prayed through the night. He would have stayed. But the Church of his day was sick in ways that were hard to miss.
Church offices were bought and sold, a corruption known as simony. Clergy were living double lives.

teach.h: BLUNT LETTERS, AND BLUNT WITH HIMSELF.
teach.b: Peter wrote letters that named things plainly, and the popes kept calling him to help with reform.

teach.h: CALLED TO HELP, LONGING FOR HIS CELL.
teach.b: He was made a cardinal and bishop and, tradition says, asked more than once to go back to his cell. What makes him worth remembering isn't just that he was blunt. Plenty of people are.
It's that he aimed the same honesty at himself. That signature was not a pose.

teach.h: BETTER ARE THE WOUNDS OF A FRIEND.
teach.b: The book of Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, has a line for this kind of friend: "Better are the wounds of a friend, than the deceitful kisses of an enemy." His letters could wound.

He wrote them because he loved the Church, not to win. The Church later named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone. Blunt love tells the truth, includes itself in the problem, and stays to help fix it.

how: Catholics keep 21 February as the memorial of Saint Peter Damian, bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his letters and writings on prayer are read in the Liturgy of the Hours and by those interested in Church reform.

o: a hermit who never left his cell to speak
a pope who sold church offices for money
a monk who wrote hard letters out of love

s: Peter Damian was born into wealth and power
tradition says he was an orphan who looked after pigs until a brother paid for his schooling.
he aimed his bluntness at himself too
he signed his letters, tradition says, Peter the sinner, monk.
he sought out high office in Rome

games.q: you're a monk who loves silence. the Church around you is selling its offices, and the pope asks for your help. what do you do?
o: stay in your cell and pray about it.
write plainly, name the corruption, and go where you're sent.
write a polite letter that offends no one.
games.why: Peter Damian wrote blunt letters, served as cardinal and bishop, and still longed for his hermitage.

practice: Think of one thing that's gone a little crooked, at work, in a group you belong to, or in your own habits, and name it privately in plain words, the way Peter Damian would.

Then do what he did with his signature: find your own part in it, however small. If you pray, bring it to God and ask for the courage to say it kindly; if you don't, let it sit, named, while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Peter Damian. A hermit monk and reformer, later a cardinal and Doctor of the Church, who wrote hard letters out of love and called himself Peter the sinner.

orig.note: Latin: Peter, sinner, monk. the way tradition says he signed his letters.

carryVoice: Your line: blunt love. Honest with others, and first with himself. Day nine hundred seventy.
